### A Successful Transformation — Tick Counts in Otters

As well as spraints, our otter dataset also contains a `tick_count` variable — 
the number of ticks recorded on each otter during the survey. Like parasite 
counts, tick counts are **right-skewed** — most otters have very few ticks, 
but a small number have many. This makes it a good candidate for log 
transformation.

```{r tick-transform, fig.cap="Figure 4. Raw (left) vs log-transformed (right) tick counts. Unlike the parasite data, the log transformation successfully normalises the tick count data.", fig.width=10, fig.height=4}

# Apply log transformation
otter_data <- otter_data %>%
  mutate(log_tick_count = log(tick_count + 1))

# Before
plot_tick_raw <- ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Tick count", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Before: raw tick counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

# After
plot_tick_log <- ggplot(otter_data, aes(x = log_tick_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = "#7CAE00", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Log(tick count + 1)", y = "Frequency",
       title = "After: log-transformed tick counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

plot_tick_raw + plot_tick_log
```

```{r tick-shapiro}
# Shapiro-Wilk before transformation
shapiro.test(otter_data$tick_count)

# Shapiro-Wilk after transformation
shapiro.test(otter_data$log_tick_count)
```

::: {.callout-note}
Notice that after log transformation, the Shapiro-Wilk test returns **p = 0.112** 
— the data are now approximately normally distributed and a parametric test would 
be appropriate. This contrasts with the parasite count data, where the large 
number of zeros meant the transformation was less successful.

This illustrates an important point — **log transformation works best when zeros 
are rare**. When a large proportion of the data are zeros (as with the parasite 
counts), a non-parametric test is often the better choice.
:::

**Comparing the tick count results with the parasite count results, what does 
this tell us about when log transformation is most effective?**

`r longmcq(c(
answer = "Log transformation works best when the data are right-skewed but zeros are relatively rare — when many values are zero, the transformation is less likely to achieve normality.",
"Log transformation always works regardless of how many zeros are in the data.",
"Log transformation only works on continuous variables, not count data.",
"Log transformation is equally effective for all right-skewed datasets."
))`
